live_web_research.page_text: [2610.11735] Onboard Marine Anomaly Detection on $Φ$sat-2: From Simulation-Based Development to In-Orbit Demonstration Skip to main content Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.11735 (cs) [Submitted on 8 Oct 2026] Title: Onboard Marine Anomaly Detection on $Φ$sat-2: From Simulation-Based Development to In-Orbit Demonstration Authors: Clotilde Szywala , Thomas Goudemant , Marjorie Bellizzi , Benjamin Francesconi , Adrien Girard View a PDF of the paper titled Onboard Marine Anomaly Detection on $\Phi$sat-2: From Simulation-Based Development to In-Orbit Demonstration, by Clotilde Szywala and 4 other authors View PDF Abstract: Onboard Artificial Intelligence can improve responsiveness and bandwidth efficiency of Earth Observation systems by processing data directly on the satellite. This paper presents the experience gained from the development, onboard integration, and post-launch adaptation of a lightweight marine anomaly detection pipeline deployed on the European Space Agency's $\Phi$sat-2 mission. The application combines sea segmentation, self-supervised feature encoding of marine regions, generic anomaly detection based on deviations from a normal sea state, and optional characterization of selected anomaly types. Before launch, the pipeline was trained and validated on simulated $\Phi$sat-2 imagery to assess algorithmic performance and compatibility with resource-constrained onboard hardware. After integration and functional validation in the mission environment, early experiments on real $\Phi$sat-2 acquisitions revealed a significant mismatch between simulated and in-orbit data. The pipeline was therefore retrained on real Level-1 imagery using an improved annotation strategy to better handle ambiguous marine regions, substantially enhancing performance. Beyond demonstrating the onboard feasibility of the application, the $\Phi$sat-2 experience highlights the importance of robust annotation strategies and sensor-aware design, and shows that simulation-based development is valuable for pre-flight risk reduction, while reliable scientific validation requires representative in-orbit data and should be clearly distinguished from functional validation. article.body:
# Φsat-2 marine anomaly system retrained after in-orbit data mismatch

A marine anomaly-detection pipeline developed for the European Space Agency’s Φsat-2 mission was retrained on real satellite imagery after early in-orbit tests exposed a significant mismatch with simulated data, according to a paper submitted to arXiv on Oct. 8.

The paper describes the development, onboard integration and post-launch adaptation of the lightweight system. Its authors — Clotilde Szywala, Thomas Goudemant, Marjorie Bellizzi, Benjamin Francesconi and Adrien Girard — say the pipeline was deployed on Φsat-2 and combines sea segmentation, self-supervised feature encoding of marine regions and anomaly detection based on deviations from a normal sea state. It can also characterize selected types of anomaly.

Before launch, the system was trained and validated using simulated Φsat-2 imagery. The authors say that work assessed algorithmic performance and compatibility with resource-constrained onboard hardware. After integration and functional validation in the mission environment, early experiments using actual Φsat-2 acquisitions showed that the simulated data did not adequately match in-orbit imagery.

The team then retrained the pipeline using real Level-1 imagery and an improved annotation strategy designed to handle ambiguous marine regions. The authors report that this substantially enhanced performance, but the abstract does not provide quantitative results.

The paper distinguishes functional validation from scientific validation: confirming that the system works in the mission environment did not establish its performance on representative in-orbit data. The authors say the experience highlights the importance of robust annotation and sensor-aware design, while describing simulation-based development as useful for reducing pre-flight risk.

The work documents a cycle from simulated-data development to adaptation after launch; it does not provide performance figures in the available abstract.
